identification: Set of five matching Tasmanian 'Peddle' pattern kitchen/cottage chairs, c1890-1910: wide curved crest rail, five ring-turned spindles, shaped 'jawbone' side supports that flare wide where they meet the seat (photo 6), deep shaped saddle seats with a scalloped front, ring-turned splayed legs with H-stretchers. This exact form (crest rail, five ring-turned spindles, jawbone supports, saddle seat, ring-turned legs, H-stretcher) matches the George Peddle chairs sold at Leski in 2024-26 (lot 323 photo checked side by side). Timber reads as figured golden blackwood on seats and legs from colour and figure, though the seats are lighter and the grain more open/oval-figured than the darker Leski examples, so English elm/ash cannot be ruled out from photos. Top rails are paler and worn (photo 4). Original patina, normal wear, no breaks seen. George Peddle (High Wycombe-trained, arrived Tasmania 1884, worked Hobart then Launceston/Nabowla) made these Windsor-style chairs in blackwood; his brother-in-law Harry Hearn made similar chairs, so attribution is by form, not stamp.

viewing_check: Most important: confirm timber on the seat underside and inside of legs (blackwood is golden to chocolate brown, fine even pores, often figured/curly, heavy; elm has coarse open zig-zag pores; ash is pale with clear ring-porous bands). Look under seats for any stamp, pencil marks or Peddle/Hearn brand, and check whether all five are truly matching (same turnings, same seat shape). Check jawbone supports for cracks or nails, seat splits, loose stretchers, replaced legs (one Leski chair had a replacement leg), and whether the paler top rails are a different timber or just worn finish.
